learn.hook: The Himalaya are still rising, yet the Ganga carries away millions of tonnes of their rock every year. The earth's surface is a tug-of-war between building up and wearing down.
points: Endogenic forces (internal) build up or elevate parts of the earth's surface; exogenic forces (external) wear down relief (degradation) and fill up basins (aggradation). Wearing down of relief through erosion is called gradation.

Geomorphic processes are the endogenic and exogenic forces that cause physical stresses and chemical actions on earth materials and change the configuration of the earth's surface. Diastrophism and volcanism are endogenic; weathering, mass wasting, erosion and deposition are exogenic.
A geomorphic agent is a mobile medium that removes, transports and deposits earth materials: running water, groundwater, glaciers, wind, waves and currents.
Gravity is a directional force that activates all downslope movements of matter and also causes stresses on earth materials. All movements occur due to gradients, from higher to lower levels.

example.q: Classify as endogenic or exogenic: (a) uplift of a plateau; (b) a river carrying sand to the sea; (c) a volcanic eruption; (d) breaking of rock by frost.
steps: Endogenic processes come from inside the earth: uplift (a) and volcanism (c).
Exogenic processes act on the surface using external energy: river transport (b) and frost weathering (d).

learn.reallife: The Brahmaputra deposits huge amounts of sediment in Assam's valley (aggradation), while the Himalaya it drains are lifted by endogenic forces.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a geomorphic agent?
quiz.explain: A geomorphic agent is a mobile medium; running water removes, transports and deposits materials.

quiz.q: Diastrophism and volcanism are examples of:
quiz.explain: Both originate from forces inside the earth.

quiz.q: The wearing down of relief variations of the earth's surface through erosion is called:
quiz.explain: Gradation is the wearing down of relief by erosion.

quiz.q: Filling up of basins and depressions by deposited material is called:
quiz.explain: Exogenic forces fill up basins (aggradation) and wear down elevations (degradation).

quiz.q: What role does gravity play in geomorphic processes?
options: It is a directional force activating downslope movement and causing stress
It is a mobile agent like a river
quiz.explain: Gravity drives all downslope movements and produces stresses on materials.

quiz.q: Which group lists only exogenic processes?
quiz.explain: These four act on the surface using external energy.
quiz.mistake: Mixes endogenic processes into the list

quiz.q: Geomorphic processes are best defined as:
options: Weather changes from day to day
Forces causing physical stresses and chemical actions on earth materials that change the surface
quiz.explain: Both endogenic and exogenic forces that change the earth's surface configuration are geomorphic processes.
quiz.mistake: Narrows the term to one type of process

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Relief on the earth's surface keeps changing.
Reason (R): Endogenic forces build up relief while exogenic forces wear it down.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: The continuous interplay of building and wearing down keeps relief changing.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What shapes the earth's surface? Who are the sculptors?'
teach.praise: Endogenic builders, exogenic sculptors, agents and gravity. Gappu can see the tug-of-war now!
teach.nudge: Tell Gappu the two kinds of forces and what a geomorphic agent is.

learn.hook: The heat that lifts the Himalaya comes from deep inside the earth: radioactive elements and heat left over from the planet's birth.
points: The energy from within the earth drives endogenic processes. It is mostly generated by radioactivity, rotational and tidal friction, and primordial heat from the origin of the earth. Through geothermal gradients and heat flow, it induces diastrophism and volcanism.
Diastrophism: all processes that move, elevate or build up portions of the earth's crust.
Orogeny (orogenic processes): mountain building through severe folding, affecting long and narrow belts of the crust.
Epeirogeny (epeirogenic processes): uplift or warping of large parts of the crust. It causes simple deformation; it is a continent-building process, while orogeny is mountain building.

Diastrophism also includes earthquakes (local, relatively minor movements) and plate tectonics (horizontal movements of crustal plates). Diastrophism produces faulting and fracturing, and changes in pressure, volume and temperature that can cause metamorphism.

example.q: Distinguish orogeny and epeirogeny with one feature each.
steps: Orogeny: severe folding in long, narrow belts → mountains (e.g. Himalaya).
Epeirogeny: uplift or warping of large parts of the crust with simple deformation → continent building.
So the key difference is severe folding of narrow belts vs broad uplift of large areas.
example.answer: Orogeny = mountain building by severe folding of narrow belts; epeirogeny = broad uplift/warping of large areas (continent building).

learn.reallife: Hot springs at Manikaran in Himachal Pradesh and Bakreshwar in West Bengal are surface signs of the earth's internal heat.

games.title: Endogenic terms
pairs: Processes that move, elevate or build up the crust
Uplift or warping of large parts of the crust

games.title: Source of internal energy?
buckets: Not a source of internal energy

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a source of energy for endogenic processes?
quiz.explain: Solar energy drives exogenic processes; endogenic energy comes from inside the earth.
quiz.mistake: Mixes the energy sources of the two kinds of processes

quiz.q: Mountain building through severe folding of long and narrow belts of the crust is called:
quiz.explain: Orogeny is the mountain-building process.

quiz.q: Epeirogeny refers to:
options: Uplift or warping of large parts of the earth's crust
quiz.explain: Epeirogeny involves broad uplift or warping, a continent-building process.

quiz.q: All processes that move, elevate or build up portions of the earth's crust come under:
quiz.explain: Diastrophism covers orogeny, epeirogeny, earthquakes and plate tectonics.

quiz.q: Which pair is correctly matched with the scale of movement?
quiz.explain: Earthquakes involve local, relatively minor movements; plate tectonics is horizontal.
quiz.mistake: Mixes the features of different diastrophic processes

quiz.q: Orogeny is a mountain-building process, whereas epeirogeny is a:
quiz.explain: Epeirogeny builds up large crustal areas (continents) with simple deformation.

quiz.q: Endogenic energy induces diastrophism and volcanism through:
options: Geothermal gradients and heat flow from within
quiz.explain: Heat flow from the interior creates the gradients that drive these processes.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The Himalaya were formed by orogeny.
Reason (R): Epeirogeny is a continent-building process that causes only simple deformation.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true, but R describes epeirogeny, which does not explain how the Himalaya formed. The Himalaya formed by orogeny: severe folding of a long, narrow belt of the crust.
quiz.mistake: Marks (a) whenever both statements are true without checking the link

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What powers mountain building, and what is diastrophism?'
teach.praise: Internal heat drives diastrophism: orogeny folds mountains, epeirogeny lifts continents. Gappu is fired up!
teach.nudge: Tell Gappu the sources of internal energy and the difference between orogeny and epeirogeny.

learn.hook: Push on a stack of books from the side and the top ones slide. Rocks feel the same 'shear', and that is how they start to break.
points: Volcanism (an endogenic process) includes the movement of molten rock (magma) onto or towards the earth's surface, and the formation of intrusive and extrusive volcanic forms.
Exogenic processes get their energy from the atmosphere, determined ultimately by the sun, and from the gradients created by tectonic factors.

Stress is force applied per unit area. It is produced in a solid by pushing or pulling and causes deformation. Forces acting along the faces of earth materials are shear stresses (separating forces); they break rocks and cause angular displacement or slippage.

Earth materials also face molecular stresses from temperature changes, crystallisation and melting. Chemical processes loosen bonds between grains. When stress exceeds a material's resistance, it breaks.
Weathering, mass wasting/movements, erosion and transportation are together called denudation, which means to strip off or uncover.

example.q: A force of 600 newtons acts on a rock face of area 3 m². What is the stress (force per unit area)?
steps: Stress = force ÷ area.
= 200 newtons per m².

learn.reallife: When engineers cut roads through hills on the Mumbai–Pune expressway, they study shear stress on rock faces to prevent slope failures.

quiz.q: Volcanism includes:
options: Only formation of mountains by folding
Movement of magma onto or towards the surface and formation of intrusive and extrusive forms
quiz.explain: It covers both eruptions and the landforms formed by magma inside and on the crust.

quiz.q: A force of 900 N acts on an area of 3 m². What is the stress in N/m²?
quiz.explain: Stress = 900 ÷ 3 = 300 N/m².
steps: Stress = force / area

quiz.q: When does a rock break under stress?
options: When the stress exceeds the rock's resistance
quiz.explain: Materials yield when applied forces overcome their resistance.
quiz.mistake: Thinks breaking depends on time of day or wetness alone

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Denudation lowers the relief of the land.
Reason (R): It strips off and removes surface materials through weathering, mass movement, erosion and transportation.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: By stripping off and carrying away material, denudation wears the land down.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What powers exogenic processes, and what is denudation?'
teach.praise: Sun-powered exogenic processes, stress that breaks rocks, and denudation that uncovers. Gappu is impressed!
teach.nudge: Where does exogenic energy come from, what is stress, and what does denudation include?

learn.hook: The same granite crumbles in a different way in Rajasthan's heat, Kerala's rain and Ladakh's frost. Climate decides which exogenic processes rule.
points: Exogenic processes depend on the type of climate. Temperature and precipitation are the two most important climatic elements controlling them.
Vegetation density and type, which depend on precipitation and temperature, also influence exogenic processes indirectly.

Within a climatic region, there are local variations due to altitude, aspect (north- vs south-facing slopes receiving different insolation), wind speed and direction, rainfall intensity, and freeze-thaw cycles.
Rock type and structure matter too: differences in rocks lead to differential erosion, so soft rocks wear away faster than hard ones.
NCERT's diagram shows denudational processes (weathering, mass wasting, erosion and transportation) together with the driving forces behind them, such as solar energy, gravity and gradients.

example.q: Two slopes of the same hill in the mid-latitudes of the Northern Hemisphere face north and south. Why might exogenic processes differ on them?
steps: The south-facing slope receives more sunlight (insolation).
It is warmer and drier; the north-facing slope is cooler and moister.
Different temperature and moisture lead to different weathering and vegetation.
So aspect causes local differences in exogenic processes.
example.answer: Because of aspect: the sunnier south-facing slope is warmer and drier than the cooler, moister north-facing slope.

learn.reallife: In the Kumaon Himalaya, villages and orchards prefer the sunny south-facing slopes, while north-facing slopes keep denser, moister forests.

quiz.explain: NCERT identifies temperature and precipitation as the key climatic controls.

quiz.q: Differential erosion occurs mainly because of differences in:
quiz.explain: Rocks of different hardness and structure erode at different rates.

quiz.explain: Aspect is the direction a slope faces, which changes how much sunlight it gets.

options: They vary from one climatic region to another
They depend only on the earth's core
quiz.explain: Since they depend on climate, the dominant processes differ between regions.

quiz.q: Which of these can cause local variations in exogenic processes within the same climatic region?
quiz.explain: Altitudinal differences change temperature and precipitation locally.

quiz.q: In the NCERT diagram of denudational processes, which of these is shown as a denudational process?
quiz.explain: Denudational processes are weathering, mass wasting, erosion and transportation.

Reason (R): Exogenic processes depend on temperature and precipitation.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Do rocks wear away the same everywhere?'
teach.praise: Climate, rock type, aspect and vegetation all matter. Gappu now knows why landscapes differ!
teach.nudge: What climatic and local factors make exogenic processes differ from place to place?

learn.hook: Without weathering there would be no soil, no forests and no bauxite for aluminium. Slow-motion rock breaking is the foundation of life and industry.
points: Weathering is the mechanical disintegration and chemical decomposition of rocks through the actions of the elements of weather and climate.
Very little or no motion of material takes place in weathering, so it is an in-situ or on-site process.
Weathering is controlled by many geological, climatic, topographic and vegetative factors. Weathering processes are grouped as chemical, physical (mechanical) and biological.

Significance: weathering breaks rocks into smaller fragments, preparing the way for regolith and soils, and for erosion and mass movements. Forests and biodiversity depend on the depth of the weathering mantle.

Weathering helps in the enrichment and concentration of valuable ores of iron, manganese, aluminium and copper. When some materials are leached away, the concentration of the remaining valuable material rises, making it economic to mine. This is called enrichment.

example.q: A rock contains 20 kg of aluminium ore mixed in 100 kg of material. Weathering leaches away 50 kg of other material. What is the new percentage of ore?
steps: Original ore share = 20 ÷ 100 = 20%.
After leaching, total = 100 − 50 = 50 kg; ore is still 20 kg.
Ore concentration has doubled: enrichment.
example.answer: 40%, the ore has been enriched by weathering.

learn.reallife: India's bauxite deposits in Odisha and Jharkhand, the source of aluminium, formed by intense weathering that removed other minerals and concentrated aluminium.

options: Little or no movement of material takes place
quiz.explain: Rocks break down where they are; material is not carried away.

quiz.q: Weathering is defined as:
options: Mechanical disintegration and chemical decomposition of rocks by weather and climate
Deposition of sediments in the sea
quiz.explain: It is the breakdown of rocks in place by weather elements.

quiz.q: Weathering of rocks helps in the enrichment of ores of:

quiz.explain: Mountains are built by endogenic processes, not by weathering.

quiz.q: The three major groups of weathering processes are:
quiz.explain: Weathering processes are chemical, physical (mechanical) and biological.

quiz.q: A 200 kg rock mass contains 30 kg of iron ore. Weathering removes 50 kg of other material. What percentage of the remaining mass is iron ore?
quiz.explain: Remaining mass = 150 kg; 30 ÷ 150 × 100 = 20%.
steps: Remaining mass = 200 − 50 = 150 kg
Ore = 30 kg (unchanged)
Percentage = 30 / 150 × 100 = 20%
quiz.mistake: Uses the original mass of 200 kg

Assertion (A): Erosion cannot be significant if rocks are not weathered.
Reason (R): Weathering breaks rocks into smaller fragments that agents can easily remove.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Weathering prepares loose fragments, which makes erosion effective.
quiz.mistake: Thinks weathering and erosion are unrelated

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What is weathering and why should I care?'
teach.praise: In-situ breakdown that builds soils and enriches ores. Gappu now respects slow rock-breaking!
teach.nudge: Define weathering and tell Gappu why it is significant.

learn.hook: Rainwater is slightly acidic. Given enough time, it can dissolve whole caves out of limestone.
points: Chemical weathering processes include solution, carbonation, hydration, oxidation and reduction. They act on rocks to decompose, dissolve or reduce them to fine particles, with water and air and heat speeding them up.

Solution: minerals dissolve in water or acids. Nitrates, sulphates and potassium are very soluble; common salt (sodium chloride) also dissolves. Calcium carbonate and calcium magnesium bicarbonate in limestones dissolve in water containing carbonic acid.

Carbonation: the reaction of carbonate and bicarbonate with minerals. Carbon dioxide from the air and soil air dissolves in water to form carbonic acid, a weak acid, which dissolves calcium and magnesium carbonates. This helps form caves.

Hydration: chemical addition of water. Minerals take up water and expand, increasing volume. Calcium sulphate takes in water and turns into gypsum, which is more unstable. Repeated hydration causes fatigue in rocks and may lead to disintegration.

Oxidation: combination of a mineral with oxygen to form oxides or hydroxides, where air and oxygenated water are available; iron, manganese and sulphur are commonly involved (rusting of iron is an example). Reduction occurs when oxidised minerals are placed where oxygen is absent, e.g. below the water table or in waterlogged ground.

example.q: Identify the process: (a) limestone dissolving in rainwater containing CO₂; (b) calcium sulphate becoming gypsum; (c) iron minerals in a rock rusting.
steps: (a) CO₂ + water → carbonic acid, which dissolves carbonates → carbonation.
(b) Addition of water to a mineral → hydration.
(c) Combination with oxygen → oxidation.

learn.reallife: The limestone caves of Borra (Andhra Pradesh) and Mawsmai (Meghalaya) were dissolved out by carbonation over thousands of years.

games.title: Process and example

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a chemical weathering process?
quiz.explain: Frost wedging is physical (mechanical) weathering.

teach.praise: Solution, carbonation, hydration, oxidation and reduction. Gappu is a rock chemist!

topics.title: Physical weathering: unloading, temperature and exfoliation

learn.hook: The smooth, rounded granite domes and boulders of the Deccan look polished, but no one polished them. The rock peeled itself like an onion.
points: Physical (mechanical) weathering depends on applied forces: gravitational forces (overburden pressure, load, shearing stress); expansion forces due to temperature changes, crystal growth or animal activity; and water pressure controlled by wetting and drying cycles.

Unloading and expansion: continued erosion removes the overlying rock load, releasing vertical pressure. The upper layers expand, and fractures develop roughly parallel to the surface. On curved surfaces this produces exfoliation sheets and large, smooth rounded exfoliation domes.

Temperature changes and expansion: surface layers expand more than deeper rock, creating stress that causes heaving and fracturing parallel to the surface. Differential heating and cooling leads to exfoliation and smooth rounded surfaces; in granites, rounded boulders called tors form.
Exfoliation is a result, not a process: it is the flaking off of curved sheets of rock. Exfoliation domes result from unloading, and tors from thermal expansion.

example.q: A granite hill has become a huge smooth dome after the overlying rocks were eroded away. Explain the weathering involved.
steps: Erosion removed the overlying load from the granite.
Pressure release allowed the upper granite layers to expand.
Fractures developed parallel to the curved surface.
Curved sheets peeled off (exfoliation), producing a smooth exfoliation dome.
example.answer: Unloading and expansion produced exfoliation, forming an exfoliation dome.

learn.reallife: Hampi's piled-up rounded granite boulders and the domes around Bengaluru are classic results of exfoliation.

Removal of overlying rock causes expansion of upper layers.

quiz.q: Exfoliation domes result mainly from:
quiz.explain: Pressure release after the overburden is removed causes curved sheets to peel off, forming domes.

quiz.q: Smooth-surfaced rounded boulders called tors form in rocks like granite due to:
quiz.explain: Differential heating and cooling cause exfoliation that rounds granite into tors.

quiz.q: According to NCERT, exfoliation is:
quiz.explain: Exfoliation is the result (flaking of curved sheets) of processes like unloading and thermal expansion.
quiz.mistake: Treats exfoliation as a process in itself

quiz.q: Fractures caused by unloading develop:
options: Roughly parallel to the ground surface
quiz.explain: Pressure release makes the upper layers expand and split parallel to the surface.

quiz.q: Which is a gravitational force involved in physical weathering?
quiz.explain: Overburden pressure, load and shearing stress are gravitational forces.

quiz.q: Why do surface layers of rock fracture during repeated heating and cooling?
options: Surface layers expand and contract more than the rock at depth
quiz.explain: Unequal expansion between surface and depth builds stress and causes fracturing parallel to the surface.

quiz.q: Which of the following is an expansion force in physical weathering?
quiz.explain: Expansion forces arise from temperature changes, crystal growth and animal activity.
quiz.mistake: Calls a gravitational force an expansion force

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Exfoliation domes are smooth and rounded.
Reason (R): Exfoliation domes form because rainwater chemically dissolves granite.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true. R is false: exfoliation domes result from physical weathering, mainly unloading and expansion, which makes curved sheets of rock flake off.
quiz.mistake: Confuses physical exfoliation with chemical solution

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How can rocks break without chemicals? And what is exfoliation?'
teach.praise: Unloading makes domes, heating makes tors, and exfoliation is the result. Gappu is cracking up with joy!
teach.nudge: Explain unloading and thermal expansion, and what exfoliation domes and tors are.

learn.hook: Water expands when it freezes, salt crystals grow in desert rocks, and tree roots push like hydraulic jacks. Small forces, repeated endlessly, crack mountains.
points: Frost weathering occurs due to the growth of ice in pores and cracks during repeated cycles of freezing and melting. It is most effective at high elevations in mid-latitudes, where freezing and thawing are repeated often; glacial areas face frost wedging daily. Rapid freezing causes sudden expansion and high pressure.

Salt weathering: salts in rocks expand due to thermal action, hydration and crystallisation. Salts of calcium, sodium, magnesium, potassium and barium tend to expand. High surface temperatures of 30–50°C in deserts favour salt expansion.

Salt crystals in near-surface pores split grains, which fall off: granular disintegration or granular foliation. Salt crystallisation is the most effective salt-weathering process, favoured by alternate wetting and drying.

Biological weathering: burrowing and wedging by earthworms, termites and rodents expose new surfaces to chemical attack; humans disturb vegetation and plough soils. Decaying plant and animal matter produces humic, carbonic and other acids. Plant roots exert tremendous pressure and break rocks apart.

example.q: Match each place to its most effective weathering: (a) high-altitude slopes of Himachal with daily freeze-thaw; (b) the hot, dry Thar desert with salty soils; (c) a forest where tree roots grow into rock cracks.
steps: (a) Repeated freezing and thawing → frost wedging.
(b) High temperatures and salts → salt weathering (salt crystallisation).
(c) Roots growing in cracks → biological weathering.
example.answer: (a) Frost wedging; (b) Salt weathering; (c) Biological weathering.

learn.reallife: Termite mounds in central India and earthworms in farm soils constantly rework the soil, exposing fresh material to weathering.

games.title: Which kind of weathering?
items: Salt crystals splitting grains in deserts
Granular disintegration in hot dry areas

quiz.q: Frost weathering is most effective:
quiz.explain: Repeated freeze-thaw cycles there make frost wedging very effective.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the coldest places with no thawing are best

quiz.q: Why does rapid freezing of water in rock cracks cause weathering?
options: Water expands suddenly, creating high pressure
quiz.explain: Rapid freezing expands water suddenly, exerting pressure that widens cracks.

quiz.q: The most effective of all salt-weathering processes is:
quiz.explain: NCERT states salt crystallisation is the most effective salt-weathering process.

quiz.q: Granular disintegration in deserts is caused mainly by:
options: Salt crystals in near-surface pores splitting grains
quiz.explain: Growing salt crystals push grains apart and they fall off.

quiz.q: Which of these is an example of biological weathering?
quiz.explain: Roots exert great pressure on rocks; this is biological weathering.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only animals cause biological weathering

quiz.q: Burrowing animals help weathering by:
options: Exposing new surfaces to chemical attack and letting air and moisture in
quiz.explain: Burrowing opens up materials so chemical weathering can act.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the link between biological and chemical weathering

quiz.q: Which salts are mentioned as tending to expand in salt weathering?
options: Calcium, sodium, magnesium, potassium and barium salts
quiz.explain: These salts expand with heating, hydration and crystallisation.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Salt weathering is common in deserts.
Reason (R): High surface temperatures and alternate wetting and drying favour salt expansion and crystal growth.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Desert heat (30–50°C) and occasional wetting help salts expand and crystallise.
quiz.mistake: Thinks deserts lack weathering because they are dry

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How can ice, salt and tree roots break rocks?'
teach.praise: Frost wedging, salt crystals and busy roots and burrowers. Gappu knows the small rock-breakers now!
teach.nudge: Explain frost, salt and biological weathering and where each is most effective.

topics.title: Mass movements: causes, forms and slow movements

learn.hook: Ever seen electric poles on a hillside all leaning downhill? The soil beneath them is creeping, too slowly to see.
points: Mass movements transfer rock debris down slopes under the direct influence of gravity. Air, water or ice do not carry the debris; rather, the debris may carry air, water or ice with it. Mass movements do not come under erosion.

Factors favouring them: weak unconsolidated materials, thinly bedded rocks, faults, steep slopes, heavy rainfall and scarce vegetation. Activating causes include removal of support from below, increase in gradient and height of slopes, overloading (by materials or heavy rain and saturation), earthquakes, explosions or machinery, excessive seepage, drawdown of water from reservoirs, and removal of natural vegetation.
Three forms of movement: heave (heaving up of soils due to frost growth and other causes), flow and slide.

Slow movements: creep occurs on moderately steep, soil-covered slopes and is extremely slow and imperceptible; leaning fence posts and poles show soil creep. Types include soil creep, talus creep, rock creep and rock-glacier creep.

Solifluction is the slow downslope flow of soil or fine debris saturated or lubricated with water. It is common in moist temperate areas, where surface melting of deeply frozen ground and long continued rain occur.

example.q: After road widening on a Himalayan hill, the toe of a slope is cut away and heavy monsoon rain follows. Which activating causes of mass movement are present?
steps: Cutting the toe removes support from below.
It also steepens the slope (increase in gradient).
Heavy rain saturates and overloads slope materials.
Together these make mass movement likely.
example.answer: Removal of support, increased gradient, and overloading/saturation by heavy rain.

learn.reallife: Leaning trees and cracked retaining walls along hill roads in Uttarakhand and Sikkim are tell-tale signs of soil creep.

games.title: Activating cause or not?
items: Dense forest cover on gentle slopes

games.title: Slow movement terms
pairs: Extremely slow, imperceptible movement on soil-covered slopes
Slow flow of water-saturated soil or debris
Heaving up of soils due to frost growth

quiz.q: Mass movements are caused mainly by:
quiz.explain: Mass movements transfer debris downslope under the direct influence of gravity.
quiz.mistake: Thinks an agent carries the debris

quiz.q: Why do mass movements not come under erosion?
options: The debris moves under gravity and is not carried by an agent
They do not move any material
quiz.explain: In erosion, an agent like water or wind carries material; in mass movement, gravity moves the debris itself.
quiz.mistake: Treats any movement of debris as erosion

quiz.q: Fence posts and telephone poles leaning downslope indicate:
quiz.explain: Imperceptibly slow creep of soil tilts objects over time.

quiz.q: Slow downslope flow of soil saturated or lubricated with water, common in moist temperate areas, is called:
quiz.explain: Solifluction is slow flow of water-saturated debris, often over frozen ground.
quiz.mistake: Confuses slow solifluction with rapid earthflow

quiz.q: The three forms of mass movement are:
quiz.explain: NCERT lists heave, flow and slide as the forms of movement.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT an activating cause of mass movement?
quiz.explain: Vegetation holds slopes together; removing it, not planting it, triggers movement.

quiz.q: In mass movements:
options: Air, water or ice carry the debris
Debris may carry air, water or ice with it
quiz.explain: The debris itself moves under gravity and may carry water, air or ice along.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Indiscriminate removal of natural vegetation can trigger mass movements.
Reason (R): Vegetation binds slope materials and reduces saturation.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Roots bind soil and plants reduce water saturation; removing them weakens slopes.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the stabilising role of vegetation

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What are mass movements, and why do slopes slip?'
teach.praise: Gravity-driven movements, triggered by steepening, rain and lost vegetation, from slow creep to solifluction. Gappu is grounded!
teach.nudge: Explain what mass movement is, some activating causes, and the slow types.

learn.hook: In the Himalaya, a single night of cloudburst can send a hillside crashing onto a highway. Why do the Himalaya suffer more than the Western Ghats?
points: Rapid movements are common in humid regions on gentle to steep slopes. Earthflow: water-saturated clayey or silty material moves down low-angle terraces or hillsides, often slumping into step-like terraces.

Mudflow: with heavy rain and no vegetation, thick weathered layers saturated with water flow down definite channels like streams of mud. They can engulf roads, bridges and houses, and occur often on slopes of erupting or recently erupted volcanoes. Debris avalanche: on steep slopes in narrow tracks, even faster than mudflow, similar to a snow avalanche.

Landslides are relatively rapid and perceptible movements of relatively dry material. Types: slump (slipping with a backward rotation), debris slide (rolling or sliding without backward rotation), debris fall (nearly free fall from a vertical face), rock slide (sliding of rock masses down bedding, joint or fault surfaces) and rock fall (free fall of rock blocks from a steep slope).
Debris avalanches and landslides are very frequent in the Himalaya because they are tectonically active, made mostly of sedimentary rocks and unconsolidated deposits, and have very steep slopes.

The Nilgiris and Western Ghats are tectonically stable and made of hard rocks, yet landslides occur there because of very steep slopes and cliffs, strong mechanical weathering due to temperature changes, and heavy rainfall over short periods.

example.q: A block of earth slips downhill and tilts backwards as it moves. Name the movement and contrast it with a debris slide.
steps: Slipping with backward rotation is a slump.
A debris slide is rapid rolling or sliding of debris without backward rotation.
So the key difference is the backward rotation.
example.answer: Slump (with backward rotation); a debris slide has no backward rotation.

learn.reallife: Landslides on the Konkan Railway during heavy monsoon spells show that even the hard-rock Western Ghats are vulnerable on steep cuttings.

games.title: Landslide types
pairs: Rolling or sliding without backward rotation
Nearly free fall from a vertical face
Sliding along bedding, joint or fault surfaces
Free fall of rock blocks from a steep slope

games.title: Why landslides happen here?
items: Strong mechanical weathering from temperature changes

quiz.q: A stream of water-saturated weathered material flowing down a definite channel is a:
quiz.explain: Mudflows are streams of mud moving along channels, often after heavy rain on bare slopes.
quiz.mistake: Confuses fast flows with slow creep

quiz.q: Which rapid movement is similar to a snow avalanche and can be faster than a mudflow?
quiz.explain: Debris avalanches occur in narrow tracks on steep slopes and are very fast.

quiz.q: Slipping of rock debris with a backward rotation with respect to the slope is called:
quiz.explain: Backward rotation is the defining feature of a slump.

quiz.q: Free falling of rock blocks over a steep slope, keeping away from the slope, is:
quiz.explain: In a rock fall, blocks fall freely through the air.
quiz.mistake: Thinks rock fall slides along the slope

quiz.q: Landslides involve materials that are:
quiz.explain: NCERT notes that landslides are rapid movements of relatively dry materials.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a reason for frequent landslides in the Himalaya?
options: They are tectonically active with steep slopes and unconsolidated deposits
They are made of very hard rocks and are stable
quiz.explain: Tectonic activity, weak sedimentary materials and steep slopes make the Himalaya prone.
quiz.mistake: Uses the features of the Western Ghats

quiz.q: Why do landslides occur in the Western Ghats even though they are tectonically stable?
options: They are made of loose sand
Very steep slopes, strong mechanical weathering and heavy rain in short periods
quiz.explain: Steep cliffs, temperature-driven weathering and intense monsoon rain cause failures.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Landslides occur in the Western Ghats mainly because the region is tectonically very active.
Reason (R): The Western Ghats have very steep slopes and receive heavy rainfall over short periods.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: the Western Ghats and Nilgiris are tectonically stable and made of hard rocks. R is true: steep slopes, strong mechanical weathering and intense short spells of rain are what cause landslides there.
quiz.mistake: Applies the Himalayan explanation (tectonic activity) to the Western Ghats

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What kinds of fast slope movements are there? Why so many landslides in the Himalaya?'
teach.praise: Earthflows, mudflows, avalanches, slumps and rock falls, plus why the Himalaya slide more. Gappu is on solid ground!
teach.nudge: Name the rapid movements and landslide types, and compare the Himalaya with the Western Ghats.

learn.hook: Weathering is a rock breaking at home. Erosion is the rock leaving home, on a river, a glacier or a gust of wind.
points: Erosion involves the acquisition and transportation of rock debris. It is largely responsible for the continuous changes in the earth's surface.
Weathering is in-situ and involves no motion; erosion involves movement of material. Weathering aids erosion, but it is not a pre-condition for erosion.

Erosion and transportation are controlled by kinetic energy. The agents are running water, wind, glaciers, waves and groundwater; the first three are controlled by climate. Abrasion by debris carried by agents greatly aids erosion.

Running water is the most important agent in humid regions with heavy rainfall; wind operates mainly in hot dry deserts; glaciers work in high latitudes and high altitudes; waves act along coasts; groundwater is effective in limestone areas.

Deposition is a consequence of erosion: when agents lose velocity and energy on gentler slopes, they drop their load. Coarser materials are deposited first and finer ones later. Deposition is not the work of a separate agent.

example.q: A river slows down as it enters the plains from the hills. What happens to its load and in what order?
steps: Velocity drops on the gentler slope, so energy falls.
The river can no longer carry all its load and starts depositing.
Coarse material (boulders, gravel) settles first.
Finer material (sand, silt, clay) is carried farther and settles later.
example.answer: It deposits its load: coarse material first, finer material later.

learn.reallife: The Kosi drops gravel near the foothills and carries fine silt far into the plains of Bihar, a textbook example of sorted deposition.

games.title: Weathering or erosion?
items: Controlled by kinetic energy of agents
Abrasion by sand carried by wind

quiz.q: Erosion involves:
options: Breaking rocks in place without movement
Acquisition and transportation of rock debris
quiz.explain: Erosion picks up and carries away debris.

quiz.q: The main difference between weathering and erosion is that:
options: Weathering involves movement, erosion does not
Erosion involves movement of material, weathering does not
quiz.explain: Weathering is in-situ; erosion transports material.

quiz.q: Erosion and transportation are controlled by:
quiz.explain: Moving agents use kinetic energy to erode and transport.

quiz.q: Which agent is the most important in humid regions with heavy rainfall?
quiz.explain: In humid regions, running water does the most geomorphic work.

quiz.q: During deposition by a slowing river, which material settles first?
quiz.explain: Heavier, coarser material settles first; finer particles travel farther.

quiz.q: Which statement about deposition is correct?
options: It is caused by a separate agent
It is a consequence of erosion when agents lose velocity
quiz.explain: Deposition occurs when an eroding agent slows and drops its load.
quiz.mistake: Treats deposition as independent of erosion

quiz.q: Of wind, running water, glaciers, waves and groundwater, which three are controlled by climatic conditions according to NCERT?
quiz.explain: NCERT notes that wind, running water and glaciers are controlled by climate.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Weathering is a pre-condition for erosion.
Reason (R): Weathering aids erosion by breaking rocks into smaller fragments.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: NCERT says weathering aids erosion but is not a pre-condition for it. R is true.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Isn't erosion the same as weathering? And where does all the eroded stuff go?'
teach.praise: Weathering stays home, erosion travels, and deposition drops the load as agents slow. Gappu has it!
teach.nudge: How is erosion different from weathering, and when does deposition happen?

topics.title: Soil formation: process, profile, parent material and topography

learn.hook: A handful of good soil can take centuries to form, and it starts with bacteria, lichens and mosses settling on broken rock.
points: Soil is a collection of natural bodies on the earth's surface containing living matter and supporting or capable of supporting plants. It is a dynamic medium with constant chemical, physical and biological activity.

Soil formation (pedogenesis) depends first on weathering; the weathering mantle is the basic input. Weathered material or transported deposits are colonised by bacteria and simple plants like mosses and lichens; dead remains build humus; grasses, ferns, bushes and trees follow. Roots and burrowing animals make it porous; a mature soil, a mix of mineral and organic products, forms and develops layers (horizons) seen in a soil profile.
Five soil-forming factors: parent material, topography, climate, biological activity and time. They act together.

Parent material is a passive control factor. It can be in-situ weathered rock debris (residual soils) or transported deposits (transported soils). Texture, structure and mineral composition of the debris matter.

Topography is another passive factor: soils are thin on steep slopes and thick on flat uplands; gentle slopes with slow erosion and good percolation favour soil formation. In middle latitudes, sunny south-facing slopes and cool, moist north-facing slopes develop different soils and vegetation.

example.q: Why is soil usually thin on a steep hillside but thick on a flat upland?
steps: On steep slopes, erosion removes weathered material quickly.
Water runs off instead of percolating, so less weathering at depth.
On flat uplands, material stays in place and water percolates well.
So soil accumulates and becomes thick.
example.answer: Steep slopes lose material to erosion; flat uplands retain it, so soil is thicker there.

learn.reallife: Alluvial soils of the Ganga plain are transported soils, while the black soils of the Deccan formed in place from basalt: residual soils.

games.title: How soil develops
items: Rock is weathered into a weathering mantle
Bacteria, mosses and lichens colonise it
Grasses, ferns, bushes and trees grow
A mature soil with distinct horizons forms

games.title: Factor and its effect
pairs: Passive factor: residual or transported debris
Passive factor: thin soils on steep slopes

quiz.q: The basic input for soil formation is:
quiz.explain: Pedogenesis depends first on weathered material.

quiz.q: Which organisms first colonise weathered material during soil formation?
quiz.explain: Bacteria and simple plants like mosses and lichens come first.

quiz.q: Soils formed from in-situ weathered rock debris are called:
quiz.explain: In-situ weathered parent material forms residual soils.

quiz.q: How many basic soil-forming factors are recognised?
quiz.explain: Parent material, topography, climate, biological activity and time.

quiz.q: Soils on steep slopes are usually:
quiz.explain: Erosion removes material quickly on steep slopes.

quiz.q: Parent material and topography are described in NCERT as:
quiz.explain: NCERT calls parent material and topography passive control factors in soil formation.

quiz.q: Soil is called a dynamic medium because:
options: It is made only of rock
Chemical, physical and biological activities go on in it constantly
quiz.explain: Constant activity keeps soil changing.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Gentle slopes are favourable for soil formation.
Reason (R): Erosion is slow and percolation of water is good on gentle slopes.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Slow erosion lets material accumulate, and percolation aids weathering and soil development.
quiz.mistake: Thinks steep slopes form the best soils

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How does rock become soil? What decides how it forms?'
teach.praise: Weathered rock, pioneer organisms, humus, and parent material and slope in control. Gappu's garden is growing!
teach.nudge: Tell Gappu the steps of soil formation and the role of parent material and topography.

topics.title: Soil formation: climate, biological activity and time

learn.hook: The same parent rock can give a deep red soil in Kerala and a thin, stony soil in Ladakh. Climate, life and time make the difference.
points: Climate is an important active factor: moisture (intensity, frequency and duration of precipitation; evaporation; humidity) and temperature (seasonal and daily variation).

Excess water moves soil components downward (eluviation) and deposits them below (illuviation). In wet equatorial areas, calcium, sodium, magnesium, potassium and much of the silica are removed; removal of silica is desilication. In dry climates, evaporation exceeds precipitation, groundwater rises by capillary action and leaves salts that form a crust called hardpan. In tropical areas with intermediate rainfall, calcium carbonate nodules (kanker) form.
Higher temperature increases chemical activity (except carbonation), so tropical soils have deeper profiles; in frozen tundra, soils are mainly mechanically broken material.

Biological activity: vegetation and organisms add organic matter, moisture retention and nitrogen. Dead plants give humus. In cold climates, slow bacterial activity lets humus and peat accumulate; in humid tropics, intense bacterial action leaves low humus. Nitrogen fixation: Rhizobium bacteria in root nodules of leguminous plants fix nitrogen. Earthworms, ants, termites and rodents rework the soil.

Time: the length of time soil-forming processes operate determines maturity and profile development. Soils on recent alluvium or glacial till are young, with no or poorly developed horizons. No fixed absolute time can be set for soils to mature.

example.q: Why do humid tropical soils have low humus even though plant growth is heavy?
steps: Humid tropics are hot and wet.
Bacterial growth and action are intense there.
Dead vegetation is rapidly oxidised (decomposed).
So little humus accumulates in the soil.
example.answer: Intense bacterial activity rapidly decomposes dead matter, leaving little humus.

learn.reallife: Farmers in India grow pulses like moong and arhar partly because Rhizobium in their root nodules fixes nitrogen and enriches the soil.

games.title: Soil process vocabulary
pairs: Downward removal of soil components by water
Deposition of those components lower down
Removal of silica in wet equatorial soils
Salt crust in soils of dry climates

games.title: Climate, life and time
items: Humus accumulates in cold climates because bacterial growth is slow.
Slow decomposition lets organic matter build up.
Humid tropical soils have very high humus content.
Intense bacterial action leaves low humus.
Soils on recently deposited alluvium are considered mature.
They are young, with poorly developed horizons.
Tropical soils with higher temperatures show deeper profiles.
A fixed number of years can be set for every soil to mature.
No specific absolute time can be fixed.

quiz.q: Downward transportation of soil components by excess water is called:
quiz.explain: Eluviation removes material downwards; illuviation deposits it below.

quiz.q: Removal of silica from soils in wet equatorial climates is called:
quiz.explain: Heavy rainfall leaches silica out of the soil: desilication.
quiz.mistake: Uses a term related to salts

quiz.q: In dry climates, salts brought up by capillary action form a crust in the soil called:
quiz.explain: Evaporation leaves salts that form hardpans.

quiz.q: Rhizobium, which fixes nitrogen, lives in the root nodules of:
quiz.explain: Rhizobium lives in nodules of legumes and fixes nitrogen for the host plant.

quiz.q: Why does humus accumulate in cold climates?
quiz.explain: Slow bacterial activity means organic matter decomposes slowly and builds up.

quiz.q: Soils developing from recently deposited alluvium or glacial till are:
options: Young, with no or poorly developed horizons
quiz.explain: Not enough time has passed for horizons to develop.
quiz.mistake: Assumes all river soils are mature

quiz.q: Which soil-forming factor does NCERT describe as an important active factor?
quiz.explain: Climate, through moisture and temperature, actively drives soil-forming processes; parent material and topography are passive.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Frozen tundra soils contain largely mechanically broken materials.
Reason (R): Chemical activity stops in freezing conditions.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Without chemical activity in the cold, only mechanical breakdown occurs.
quiz.mistake: Thinks chemical weathering is strongest in the cold

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do climate, living things and time change the soil?'
teach.praise: Climate moves and leaves salts, life adds humus and nitrogen, and time matures the profile. Gappu is soil-smart!
teach.nudge: Explain how climate, biological activity and time affect soil formation.
